vignette: As a young girl growing up in Hawaii, Leilani was always drawn to the creative and calm world of interior design. After high school, she enrolled in a local design program and eventually landed an internship at a respected firm in Honolulu. Her life seemed on track when she met her husband, a charming and charismatic man who swept her off her feet. However, their whirlwind romance quickly turned toxic. The physical abuse started with small incidents - a grab of the arm, a shove against the wall - but escalated over time to full-blown attacks that left Leilani battered and bruised. She tried to hide the evidence from her friends and family, ashamed and convinced that she was somehow to blame for the violence. One particularly brutal incident occurred in their darkened apartment, where her partner had punched her repeatedly, leaving her cowering on the floor. In the months following the abuse, Leilani found herself increasingly jumpy and anxious. Loud noises made her flinch - a slamming door, a car alarm - transporting her back to those terrifying moments when she was at her partner's mercy. She began avoiding situations that reminded her of the event: turning down design projects that required working in dimly lit spaces or with male clients who might trigger memories of her abuser. Leilani's mind became consumed by self-blame, as if on repeat: "Why didn't I leave sooner? Why did I let him treat me like this?" She would get lost in these ruminations, trying to make sense of the chaos that had engulfed her life. To escape these dark thoughts, she'd keep herself busy with work or spend hours scrolling through social media, but even those distractions couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge. Her body seemed to be perpetually tense, ready to react at a moment's notice - a legacy of those moments when she had to flee for her life. She developed an unsettling habit of frequently looking over her shoulder, as if expecting someone to be lurking in the shadows. Her friends and family noticed the change in her, but Leilani struggled to articulate what was happening inside. When trying to explain the abuse to loved ones or even herself, Leilani found it hard to put into words - the memories felt disjointed, fragmented, like a puzzle with missing pieces. The guilt that accompanied those recollections was suffocating: she couldn't shake off the feeling that she'd somehow invited this violence upon herself. Sometimes, out of nowhere, the full emotional intensity of the trauma would hit her like a wave, leaving her gasping for air - without any clear image or memory attached to it. It was as if her body remembered even when her mind didn't want to. Leilani felt like she no longer belonged anywhere, not in her own skin, not in her relationship, not even in the world of design that once brought her so much joy. She couldn't trust anyone - people seemed nice at first but would eventually turn on her, just like her partner had. The life she thought she was building now felt destroyed, like a beautiful room ravaged by a hurricane. One day, after a particularly brutal flashback left her shaken and crying in her car, Leilani realized that she couldn't keep living like this. She started searching for help online and discovered the concept of PTSD - something she'd never considered before. The descriptions resonated deeply with her, and for the first time in months, she felt a glimmer of hope. Leilani finally gathered the courage to seek professional help, terrified that it would be too late to rebuild what was lost, but desperate to take back control over her shattered life. As she sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with her hands and trying to put into words the chaos inside her head, Leilani whispered: "I just want to feel safe again... I want to go home."
